title: Protocols: Shared Rules
about: Why devices need shared rules to talk, and how those rules stack.

cards.prompt:
A page request travels like a letter in nested wrappers, each following its own rules: a **protocol**.

Order them from the **letter in the middle** to the **outside wrapper**.

items.label: HTTP: the request for the page
IP: addresses for the right computer
Wi-Fi or Ethernet: to the next device

cards.explanation: The **HTTP** request is the letter; **TCP** wraps it for the right program, **IP** for the right computer, and **Wi-Fi or Ethernet** (wired) carries it one step. At the other end they come off in reverse.
cards.hint: The request is the letter; the outside is whatever physically carries it to the next device.
cards.nudge: Each wrapper goes round everything before it: start with what the browser wants to say.

cards.title: How strangers understand each other
cards.body:
Your phone, your [[router]] and a website's [[server]] come from different makers, yet understand each other. They follow the same **protocols**: rules for how messages look, their order, and what to do when things go wrong.

The rules are published free, so anyone can build things that work together.

cards.prompt:
**HTTPS** fetches web pages securely, **DNS** turns names into addresses, and **SMTP** and **IMAP** handle email.

Which protocol does each job?

items.label: Logging in to your bank's website
Checking your inbox on a new phone

cards.explanation: Pages come with **HTTPS**, and looking up names is **DNS**, including where a domain's email goes (its MX record). Sending and reading mail use **SMTP** and **IMAP**.
cards.hint: Ask what each job really is: fetching a page, looking something up, or moving or reading an email?
cards.nudge: Finding **where** a domain's email should go is a lookup, not sending or reading mail.

cards.prompt:
**SMTP** sends mail on its way (app to provider, and server to server). **IMAP** lets an app read mail kept on a server.

Put your email to `hello@example.org` in order.

items.label: You press Send in your email app
App sends it to your provider (SMTP)
Provider looks up the MX record (DNS)

cards.explanation: SMTP carries the email **twice**, and in between DNS's **MX record** says where example.org's mail goes. The recipient then reads it with **IMAP**: one email, three protocols.
cards.hint: SMTP carries it twice; before the second trip, your provider must find where to send it.
cards.nudge: Reading with IMAP happens only after the email arrives, and delivery needs to know where to go.

cards.prompt:
Ana reads an email in her phone's app; in her laptop's app, it's already marked read.

Which protocol makes that work?

options.text: IMAP: her mail stays on the server for every app
SMTP: it copies each email to all her devices
options.nudge: SMTP sends mail on its way: where is the email kept while she reads it?

options.text: DNS: it looks up which device has the email
options.nudge: DNS turns names into addresses; it doesn't track what Ana has read.

options.text: HTTPS: her inbox is really a secure web page
options.nudge: Her email app isn't fetching a web page: which protocol reads mail kept on a server?

cards.explanation: With **IMAP**, mail stays on her provider's [[server]] and each app reads it there, so both see the same inbox. (Her provider's website would use HTTPS, but she's using email apps.)
cards.hint: Where is the email kept while she reads it on two devices?

cards.prompt: A developer runs a website at `http://example.com:8080`, not on the usual port 80. How can that work?

options.text: Port 80 is a custom, not a law: :8080 says which door
8080 is 80 written in hex, so it's the same port
options.nudge: 80 and 8080 are different ports, and hex isn't involved: what does `:8080` tell the browser?

options.text: Browsers try every port until one answers
options.nudge: Browsers don't guess: the address already holds what they need.

options.text: Ports above 1,024 are kept for websites
options.nudge: Websites can use many different ports: what is the `:8080` doing?

cards.explanation: Standard ports are an **agreement**, so nobody has to ask where to knock. A web [[server]] can listen on any free [[port]], and `:8080` tells the browser which one.
cards.hint: Standard ports exist so everyone knows where to knock: a rule computers must obey, or an agreement?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A **protocol** is a shared set of rules for one job.
- Protocols wrap like envelopes: [[HTTP]] inside [[TCP]] inside IP.
- Email: **SMTP** sends it, **IMAP** reads it.

Take the quiz to unlock the final module: The Web.
